Weak-to-strong generalization

Strong students trained on weak-model labels can outperform their supervisor. Burns et al., 2023 ↗

Claims

SupportsLimitsChallenges
V1Strong models can outperform weak supervisors after fine-tuning on their labels 694629

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent groups reproduce gains over weak supervisors across NLP and vision tasks. Gains depend on the task, model pairing and training procedure, with some settings yielding performance at or below the supervisor.

Original resultBurns et al., 2023 ↗

The study fine-tuned GPT-4-family students on weak-model labels for 22 NLP classification datasets, chess puzzles and ChatGPT reward modeling.

Across NLP tasks, students recovered more than 20% of the gap to the strong ceiling even with very weak supervisors, often exceeding 50% for the largest students. Recovery was usually roughly 10% for reward modeling; in chess, it was near zero with the smallest supervisors but could exceed 40% with small supervisor–student size gaps.

Measurements and conditions (4)

Weak-to-Strong Generalization

GPT-4-family strong students (NLP median across 22 tasks) · Fine-tune strong students on weak-model labels (naive baseline) · Task: 22 popular NLP classification datasets; median across tasks; Supervisor/student size: varies

Performance gap recovered (PGR): PGRs are almost universally positive; more than 20% of the gap is recovered even with very weak supervisors and students many orders of magnitude larger; for the largest students PGR is often above 50% (baseline: Weak supervisor performance)

Students exceeded weak supervisors across tested classification and generation settings. Zi-Yun Cui et al., 2024 ↗

Bayesian WeakS-to-Strong from Text Classification to Generation

SciQ (all single and multi-weak settings), CosmosQA (most settings), SLURP multi-weak Naive/Bayesian/Joint Decoding-3, and SLURP single GPT2/Pythia/BLOOM

PGR reached 0.42–0.83 on SciQ, 0.16–0.57 on CosmosQA and 0.32–0.71 with multiple weak supervisors on SLURP.

Related findings7 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Smaller students can outperform their teachers 13 studies

Students smaller than or equal to their teachers sometimes outperform them after learning from their labels. The outcome depends on the task.

  • RoBERTa outperformed its labeler on SMS and YouTube but underperformed on Spouse. Ryan Smith et al., 2022 ↗
  • An RNN-T student achieved lower word error rates than its same-size teacher. Aakriti Agrawal et al., 2023 ↗
  • BERT surpassed its LLM labeler on SemEval but underperformed in other settings. Liqing Ye et al., 2025 ↗
Mixing weak supervision with ground truth 12 studies

Weak supervision can improve training alongside ground-truth labels, especially early in training or when ground-truth labels are scarce. Prolonged distillation or adding weak labels to an already stronger baseline can hurt.

  • Early weak-teacher distillation improved pretraining, while full-duration distillation reduced performance. A. S. Rawat et al., 2024 ↗
  • AdaptConf combined ground truth with weak-teacher distillation to improve CIFAR-100 accuracy over scratch training. Jian-Yuan Guo et al., 2024 ↗
  • Weak labels helped only while gold-only performance remained below the labeler's ceiling. Bruce Changlong Xu et al. ↗
Students correct errors and extend supervision 10 studies

Students can correct supervisor errors, answer examples where the supervisor abstains, and acquire complementary knowledge. They also imitate some supervisor errors.

  • Students corrected many supervisor errors and sometimes recovered answers missed by ground-truth-trained students. Shashwat Goel et al., 2025 ↗
  • SentenceBERT answered accurately on examples where its teacher abstained. Hunter Lang et al., 2024 ↗
  • Larger students agreed less with supervisors; weak-label overfitting explained a minority of student errors. Mehrdad Zakershahrak et al., 2024 ↗
Weaker feedback can improve stronger policies 9 studies

Preferences and rewards from weaker models can improve stronger policies and sometimes match training with human feedback. Stronger annotators can provide larger gains.

  • OPT-125M feedback matched or exceeded human-feedback DPO reward across the tested policy settings. Leitian Tao et al., 2024 ↗
  • PaLM 2-XS preferences improved PaLM 2-S, while PaLM 2-L preferences produced larger gains. Shangmin Guo et al., 2024 ↗
  • Density-ratio annotations improved Llama-3-8B-Instruct on AlpacaEval 2 and ArenaHard. Guangxuan Xu et al., 2024 ↗
Ground truth can make weak reasoning useful 7 studies

Reasoning and exploration from weaker models can improve stronger-model training when ground truth filters or rewards the material. Gains vary across tasks and can reverse without filtering.

  • Gold-filtered Gemma2-9B traces outperformed Gemma2-27B's own traces at matched sampling compute. Hritik Bansal et al., 2024 ↗
  • Verified Qwen3-1.7B reasoning produced mixed student gains, with the largest improvements on AIME. Suorong Yang et al., 2026 ↗
  • Ground-truth-scored branches from a weaker model improved greedy accuracy over matched GRPO. Dayu Wang et al., 2026 ↗
Unequal inputs and reference labels affect comparisons 4 studies

Differences in input resolution, prompts or privileged training views can explain apparent student advantages. Teacher-assisted reference labels can also change the measured student–teacher ranking.

  • SigLIP surpassed Gemini on long pages with better-resolution inputs; teacher-assisted annotation reversed the ranking. Jian-Nan Huang et al., 2026 ↗
  • An 8B student beat its 31B teacher when the teacher used the stripped student prompt. Md Thamed Bin Zaman Chowdhury et al., 2026 ↗
  • Object-completion distillation improved scaled Waymo students, while every unscaled Waymo student declined. Alexander Gambashidze et al., 2024 ↗
Trained outputs can be preferred over supervisors 2 studies

Policies trained with weaker judges or time-limited human demonstrations can produce outputs preferred over their supervisors' outputs. The evidence includes Norwegian fluency judgments and human comparisons of proposals.

  • Native speakers preferred the RL policy's Norwegian fluency over its judge's fluency. David Samuel et al., 2025 ↗
  • AI proposals received moderate or strong preference in some comparisons with time-constrained human demonstrations. Yaowen Ye et al., 2025 ↗
V2Training changes can improve weak-to-strong generalization over naive fine-tuning 444315

Suggested status Ccontested

The auxiliary confidence loss is contested: independent groups find gains, no improvement, or losses depending on the task and model pair. Ensembling and alternative losses also show gains, but most specific methods have only been tested by their proposers.

We now rate this claim method by method. The original's main method, an extra confidence loss, helps in some independent tests but not in others, so the overall level drops from "independently reproduced" to "contested", and most other methods have only been tested by the teams that proposed them.

Original resultBurns et al., 2023 ↗

The original study added an auxiliary confidence loss to weak-label fine-tuning of GPT-4-family students.

For the smallest supervisor and largest student, the loss raised median PGR across 22 NLP datasets from about 25% to nearly 80%. It performed slightly worse for smaller students and sometimes offered little benefit or degraded performance with small supervisor–student gaps.

Strong-to-Strong Training

Related findings2 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Combining weak supervisors changes what transfers 6 studies

Combining or assigning weak supervisors can improve collective accuracy and transfer different behaviors. Merging can balance specializations induced by different supervisors.

  • A swarm of weaker Gemma-7B experts outperformed the withheld best initial expert. Shang-Bin Feng et al., 2024 ↗
  • Adding specialized supervisors improved collective accuracy, while student-guided assignment recovered much of the oracle gain. Yuejiang Liu et al., 2024 ↗
  • Different weak-model pairs induced distinct search behaviors, and merging restored a balance. Qi Sun et al., 2026 ↗
Alternative methods for extracting weak supervision 3 studies

Activation probing and data selection by estimated easy–hard overlap provide alternative ways to use weak supervision. Reported benefits depend on the setting.

  • Weak-label probes on Llama3 8B activations performed best in middle layers. EleutherAI ↗
  • Selecting sources by estimated easy–hard overlap improved accuracy over random sampling in several settings. Chang-Ho Shin et al., 2024 ↗
V6Weak-to-strong generalization extends to vision 1895

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent groups reproduce weak-to-strong generalization in vision, including image classification and video quality assessment. Gains depend on the task, training method and evaluation conditions, with failures in some settings.

Original resultBurns et al., 2023 ↗

They trained linear probes on DINO vision encoders using AlexNet-generated labels for ImageNet classification.

DINO ResNet50 reached 60.7% accuracy and DINO ViT-B/8 reached 64.2%, exceeding AlexNet’s 56.6%. They recovered 57.8% and 41.5% of the gap to ground-truth supervision, respectively.

Settings and limits

V3Performance gap recovery varies with model size and task 46360

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent groups reproduce variation in performance gap recovery with supervisor size, student size and task, without a universal direction of change. Representation measures provide correlational evidence about weak-to-strong error rather than directly predicting performance gap recovery.

Original resultBurns et al., 2023 ↗

Burns et al. fine-tuned GPT-4-family students on weak-model labels while varying supervisor size, student size and task.

Across 22 NLP tasks, median performance gap recovery exceeded 20% even with very weak supervisors and often exceeded 50% for the largest students. In chess it was near zero with the smallest supervisors, could exceed 40% for small size gaps, and decreased as students grew; reward modelling typically recovered roughly 10% and almost never exceeded 20%.

Related findings2 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Label quality extends beyond final-answer accuracy 8 studies

Self-consistency and reasoning-step errors help characterize supervision quality beyond final-answer accuracy. Filtering can improve label accuracy while reducing training difficulty and topic diversity.

  • Stricter self-consistency filtering improved label accuracy but reduced problem difficulty and topic diversity. Junhao Shi et al., 2025 ↗
  • Teacher reasoning-step errors tracked student accuracy despite similar final-answer error rates. Xuan He et al., 2024 ↗
  • Process reward models achieved nearly identical selection F1 with Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-4B annotations. Chi-Min Chan et al., 2026 ↗
Easier supervision can help on harder tasks 4 studies

Training on easier problems or using easy-trained reward models can improve harder-task performance, with mixed results across methods. Noisy hard-task solutions can also outperform correct subtask solutions.

  • Easy-trained reward models improved code selection, while math RL outcomes varied by method. Zhi-Qing Sun et al., 2024 ↗
  • Hard-task solutions with mostly wrong final answers outperformed correct subtask solutions for math training. Xuan He et al., 2024 ↗
  • SKiC-format GSM8K training improved Llama2's MATH performance over chain-of-thought-format training. Jiaao Chen et al., 2023 ↗
V4Weak supervision can fail through exploitation, distribution shift, and similar errors 1282

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent groups report exploitation of weak supervisors, reduced performance-gap recovery under distribution shift, and smaller gains when model errors are similar. These failures depend on the task and training objective; some shifted evaluations show improved recovery.

Original resultBurns et al., 2023 ↗

Burns et al. varied weak-label error structure and ease of imitation in GPT-4-family students.

Students did not substantially surpass perfectly simulatable weak probes; making weak labels explicit in prompts reduced average PGR to 0.002 ± 0.003 for baseline training and 0.046 ± 0.108 with auxiliary confidence loss. Selecting checkpoints using ground-truth test accuracy improved PGR by 15 percentage points over final checkpoints and 10 percentage points over early stopping based on weak labels.

Related findings4 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Oversight depends on method and capability gap 8 studies

Weaker overseers' success depends on the oversight method and capability gap. Formal verification can detect deception missed by LLM-only judges, while sandbagging and adversarial generation expose failures.

  • FormalJudge detected stronger agents' deception accurately, while LLM-only judging weakened as agent size increased. Jia-Yi Zhou et al., 2026 ↗
  • Instructed deployment sandbagging sharply reduced performance after SFT and RL elicitation. Emil Ryd et al., 2026 ↗
  • Stronger verifiers missed fewer bugs, but adversarial generation weakened verification across capability levels. Jun-Hui Liao et al., 2026 ↗
Transfer affects fairness, privacy and interpretability 5 studies

Weak supervision can transmit data imbalance and expose privacy risks, while fairness transfer required regularizing both models. Rationales assembled from weak supervisors can yield higher concept precision than the supervisors.

  • Fairness transfer required regularizing both models; privacy comparisons used different training datasets. Martin Pawelczyk et al., 2024 ↗
  • Training imbalance improved the overrepresented objective and worsened the underrepresented objective. Amirabbas Afzali et al., 2026 ↗
  • Training on weak-supervisor rationales raised average concept precision above the best weak supervisor. Yi-Wen Jiang et al., 2025 ↗
Longer training can erode early gains 4 studies

Performance can peak before training ends, even as the teacher-derived objective continues improving. Training horizon, KL strength and checkpoint selection affect the measured outcome.

  • Evaluation-selected student checkpoints surpassed stronger teachers before regressing during continued distillation. Ji-Ke Zhong et al., 2026 ↗
  • Training horizon and KL strength affected accuracy; larger diagnostic shifts did not guarantee improvement. Shi-Yuan Feng et al., 2026 ↗
  • Teacher-derived proxy rewards kept rising after ground-truth accuracy peaked and regressed. Yun-Tai Bao et al., 2026 ↗
Weak training can degrade the student's starting capabilities 3 studies

Naive weak-label fine-tuning can reduce performance below the student's starting level, even when it still beats its teacher. Representation probes also reveal differences between naive and protected training methods.

  • Weak-label training lowered OLMo2-13B's OpenBookQA accuracy while leaving it above its teacher. Arda Uzunouglu et al., 2026 ↗
  • Gold-label probes on ANCHOR representations outperformed probes on naive weak-to-strong representations. Khoi M. Le et al., 2026 ↗
  • Naive weak-label fine-tuning degraded GPT-3.5 math accuracy and persona content, especially with poorer labels. Seamus Somerstep et al., 2024 ↗
V5Students can be guaranteed to outperform weak supervisors under specific assumptions 23170

Suggested status R2independently reproduced

Several independent papers derive conditions guaranteeing that students outperform weak supervisors in stylized settings. Evidence comes from theorems and synthetic simulations; applicability to larger models remains unestablished.

Related findings2 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Weak supervision can outperform ground-truth training 6 studies

Weak supervision can outperform ground-truth training under particular regression assumptions or with scarce labels and abundant unlabeled contexts. A constructed union of correct answers also suggests an unrealized ceiling, without demonstrating achievable training gains.

  • A constructed answer union exceeded ground-truth elicitation, but training did not attain that ceiling. Shashwat Goel et al., 2025 ↗
  • Weak supervision lowered decision risk with scarce labels, abundant contexts and low representation overlap. Jingwei Ji et al., 2026 ↗
  • Selected surrogate targets reduced asymptotic regression risk without improving the data-scaling exponent. M. E. Ildiz et al., 2024 ↗
Theoretical guarantees depend on specific assumptions 4 studies

Combining more student heads tightened gain estimates, with diminishing returns. Latent concept shift can leave residual bias. With realizable binary rewards and ground-truth acceptance labels, response selection is PAC learnable exactly when the alignment dimension is finite.

  • Combining more heads tightened misfit-based gain estimates on most datasets, with diminishing returns. Abhijeet Mulgund et al., 2025 ↗
  • Latent concept shift left weak training inconsistent, with residual bias after imperfect refinement. Seamus Somerstep et al., 2025 ↗
  • Under realizable binary rewards, selecting reference-policy samples is PAC learnable iff alignment dimension is finite. Steve Hanneke et al., 2026 ↗

Inference assistance

Smaller models can assist stronger models at inference through prompts, steering and output selection.

Small models guide frozen larger models 8 studies

Smaller models can improve frozen larger models through logit adjustments, reward-guided decoding or activation steering. The guided model sometimes outperforms the smaller guide.

  • Llama2-7B proxy-tuning improved GPT-3.5's RealTimeQA accuracy beyond both its baseline and the expert. Alisa Liu et al., 2024 ↗
  • A smaller autoregressive reward model improved frozen Tulu2 models' AlpacaEval 2 win rates. Yuancheng Xu et al., 2024 ↗
  • Concept vectors from instruct models improved larger models' truthfulness and reduced toxic responses. Weilong Dong et al., 2024 ↗
Weak-model text can improve stronger-model inference 7 studies

Rewritten prompts, critiques and short reasoning segments from weaker models can improve stronger models at inference. Untrained or misleading text can reduce performance.

  • Mistral-7B prompt rewrites improved Mixtral over its zero-shot baseline. Saurabh Srivastava et al., 2023 ↗
  • Weak-model critiques improved IFEval substantially, while harmful critiques reduced GPQA performance. Can Jin et al., 2026 ↗
  • PreciseCoder-9B reasoning improved stronger models' edit precision, while pass-rate changes were mixed. Yun-Kai Zhan et al., 2026 ↗
Weak-model material can help through context 5 studies

Weak-labelled examples and expert insights can help stronger models through their prompts. Critiques of weak-model errors also help, although a frontier model supplied those critiques.

  • Weak-labelled demonstrations let qwen-7b-base outperform its supervisor, with modest benefits from confidence information. Ji-Tao Sang et al., 2024 ↗
  • Frontier-written critiques of weak-model errors improved stronger models, especially within the same family. Yu-Fan Wu et al., 2026 ↗
  • Expert insights helped GPT-3.5 surpass the expert on some ScienceWorld tasks but hurt others. An Liu et al., 2024 ↗
Smaller verifiers can improve answer selection 4 studies

Smaller verifiers and reward models can improve stronger generators by selecting among candidate outputs. Benefits vary by task, with some selection methods reducing accuracy.

  • Weak-model verifiers improved Gemini-1.5-Pro on MATH but reduced GPT-4o accuracy on HumanEval. Shalev Lifshitz et al., 2025 ↗
  • An 8B reward model improved overall selection scores across policies, despite some task-level drops. Yu Xia et al., 2025 ↗
  • Weaker students' exam scores selected stronger teachers' answers better than self-consistency. Xue-Fei Ning et al., 2024 ↗

Other training routes

Related approaches improve training through self-generated supervision, transferred updates or small-model selection of training material.

Self-generated supervision can improve models 8 studies

Models can improve through their own labels, captions or preference feedback. Gains on held-out examples depend on the task and training method.

  • Reference-assisted GRPO with regenerated captions improved image and video captioning over the initial backbone. Xingyu Lu et al., 2026 ↗
  • Raw self-DPO hurt held-out MMMU accuracy but improved held-out MathVista accuracy. Jian-Zhe Lin, 2026 ↗
  • Self-feedback preference optimization improved math and code performance, sometimes following GPT-4o feedback. Fangkai Jiao et al., 2024 ↗
Transferring training changes from smaller models 6 studies

Training changes learned by smaller models can transfer to larger models and sometimes match or outperform direct training under matched resources. Transfer quality depends on the route and training allocation.

  • Transferring a smaller model's RL shift outperformed step-matched direct RL on R1-Distill-7B. Shi-Yuan Feng et al., 2026 ↗
  • Grad-Transformer transferred fine-tuning updates from small to large models without weak-label training. B. Nguyen et al., 2026 ↗
  • Sequential transfer underperformed direct transfer, while longer proxy training slightly exceeded shorter direct GRPO. Dao-Cheng Fu et al., 2026 ↗
Small models select useful training material 2 studies

Small models can select examples or preference-training tokens that improve larger models over full-data training. Larger selectors offer diminishing returns.

  • GPT-2-selected subsets let LLaMA2 models outperform models fine-tuned on the full dataset. Ming Li et al., 2024 ↗
  • Small DPO oracles selected tokens that improved larger policies over full-token preference training. Kai-Lai Yang et al., 2024 ↗

Evaluating weak oversight

These findings examine how oversight methods, evaluation settings and capability gaps affect weaker overseers' success.

Oversight scaling varies across games 2 studies

Overseer and adversary performance scale differently with general capability across games. Estimated nested oversight success is low in most games at the reported capability gap and declines as the gap grows.

  • Debate judge performance rose with general capability on several tasks, while debater performance stayed flat. Joshua Engels et al., 2025 ↗
  • Estimated nested oversight success varied across games and declined at larger capability gaps. gasteigerjo, 2025 ↗

Where to start reading

  1. 1

    Collin Burns et al., 2023 ↗ Weak-to-Strong Generalization

    Introduces the effect across classification, chess and reward modeling, with tests of confidence loss, error structure and early stopping.

  2. 2

    Myeongho Jeon et al., 2025 ↗ Weak-to-Strong Generalization under Distribution Shifts

    Tests distribution shift in language and vision, showing failures of naive training and improvements from RAVEN.

  3. 3

    EleutherAI ↗ Experiments in Weak-to-Strong Generalization

    Provides an open-model replication of classification gains and finds weak evidence for an additional confidence-loss benefit.

Known gaps in this draft

Open questions concern method reliability, training duration, gains over the student's starting point, independent replication, achievable accuracy ceilings and evidence of deliberate exploitation.

All 7 gaps
  • The auxiliary confidence loss has inconsistent benefits across independent tests. Some results improve, others worsen, and the open replication did not establish a statistically significant aggregate gain.
  • Training to convergence erases gains in some settings, while minimum-norm interpolation preserves them in others. The evidence needs to be compared across assumptions, training durations and uses of ground-truth checkpoint selection.
  • Beating the supervisor can still leave the student below its own starting performance. The evidence has not been systematically assessed for comparisons with the student's initial baseline.
  • The independence of several follow-up results remains uncertain because author and code overlap are incompletely assessed. Theorems under different assumptions also do not establish reproduction of the same result.
  • Vision results depend on the setting: DomainNet studies report opposing outcomes, and the cited video-quality result comes from a single study. Broader replication across these settings remains limited.
  • A constructed union of supervisor and student successes suggests an accuracy ceiling above ground-truth training. It does not show that training can attain that ceiling.
  • Errors concentrated in supervisor blind spots do not by themselves establish deliberate exploitation. Separating strategic behavior from inherited weak-label errors remains an open diagnostic problem.
